say: Meet Flow Matrix: a traffic flow network analyzer that turns road networks into mathematics.
Traffic sensors cover only some roads. Flow Matrix uses linear algebra and graph theory to estimate the unknown flows on the others.
The dashboard reads everything live from the database: total networks, total junctions, and solved networks.
Below are the saved networks, each with its size, creation method and solution status.
Create New Network offers two methods. Automatic, from a real map, or manual, drawn by hand.
For the automatic method, we search for a pickup location. Suggestions from Open Street Map data appear as we type.
Then we choose a destination, and set a demand of one hundred vehicles travelling between the two places.
Flow Matrix finds the driving route, and downloads the actual roads around it from Open Street Map.
Intersections become the vertices of a graph, and the road segments between them become directed edges. One way rules are preserved, and each edge keeps the real road shape.
To keep the system readable, points a few metres apart are merged into one junction, and dead end side streets are left out.
The network is fully editable. We can rename a junction, delete a road, or connect two junctions to add one.
Then we save it to the database.
The manual method starts with a blank canvas. Each click creates a junction.
In connect mode, clicking two junctions draws a one way road between them.
Junctions can be dragged, and their roads follow.
We name the junctions, and set the external demand. One hundred vehicles enter at A, and one hundred leave at C.
This road has a sensor, so we mark its flow as known: sixty. Every other road is an unknown, from x one to x four.
Deleting a junction also removes its roads, and the graph updates immediately.
Everything is solved on the same page. At every junction, incoming flow minus outgoing flow equals the net demand. That gives one equation per junction.
Written as A X equals B, matrix A has one row for each junction, and one column for each unknown road.
Adding the constants as an extra column gives the augmented matrix.
Gaussian elimination creates zeros below each pivot, giving row echelon form. Every row operation is shown, with the matrix after each step.
Gauss Jordan elimination then continues to the reduced row echelon form.
The rank is three, so there are three independent equations. With four unknowns, x one, x two and x three are pivot variables, and x four is free.
So there are infinitely many solutions. Calling the free value t, x one is sixty minus t, x two is forty, and x three is forty plus t.
We can enter any value for t. With t equal to ten, every road label updates.
Traffic cannot be negative. If t is too large, Flow Matrix reports that the solution is mathematically valid, but not physically possible.
The null space explains this freedom. This vector moves traffic off the road from B to C, and onto the path through D. Every junction stays balanced. That is circulating traffic.
We save the network and run the analysis, and its status changes to solved.
After reloading the page, everything is still there, read back from the database.
The dashboard statistics have updated.
Editing a saved network marks its old solution as outdated.
Deleting a network removes it, and the statistics change again.
Flow Matrix is built with React, TypeScript, Tailwind C S S and React Flow on the front end, Python and Fast A P I on the back end, and Postgres for storage.
The row reduction is our own, in exact fractions. Sim Pie verifies it independently, Num Pie and Sigh Pie check physical feasibility, and the maps come from Open Street Map.
The same conservation principle applies to traffic management, water distribution, computer networks and electrical networks.
Flow Matrix. Where mathematics meets real world networks.
